findings.title: Equal-order providers are silently and nondeterministically selected instead of failing fast
findings.body: DefaultCryptoProvider, FIPS1402Provider, and WildFlyElytronProvider all return order() 200. This change sorts providers by order and silently uses the first one, retaining ServiceLoader/classpath iteration order for ties and only logging the ignored providers at debug level. If the default and FIPS providers, or Elytron and default providers, accidentally coexist on the classpath, the selected provider is therefore classpath-dependent; in particular a non-FIPS provider can silently be selected in an environment expecting FIPS cryptography. Previously detection failed fast when multiple providers were present. A tie for the highest order should still fail, or the mutually exclusive server providers should have distinct deterministic priorities.

findings.title: New abstract order() method breaks existing CryptoProvider implementations
findings.body: Adding abstract int order() to the public CryptoProvider interface is source- and binary-incompatible for implementations outside this repository. Existing compiled implementations will throw AbstractMethodError when CryptoIntegration invokes order() through its comparator, and existing source implementations will no longer compile. A default method, for example returning 0, would preserve compatibility while allowing the built-in providers to declare their higher precedence.

findings.title: getBouncyCastleProvider returns an unrelated JVM-default KeyStore provider
findings.body: The CryptoProvider contract states that getBouncyCastleProvider returns the BouncyCastle (or BCFIPS) provider, but this implementation returns the provider associated with KeyStore.getDefaultType(), typically SUN/SunPKCS12 and configurable through JVM security settings. Callers that use the returned provider by name or expect BouncyCastle-only services such as BCFKS or AES/CBC/PKCS7Padding can therefore fail or silently use a different provider depending on JVM configuration. If no BouncyCastle provider is available, the method should fail clearly or return null as other non-BC providers do rather than masquerading as BouncyCastle.

findings.title: ECDSA tests use one default EC key and only verify self-consistent round-tripping
findings.body: The test creates a single EC key pair without specifying a curve, so on the usual SunEC provider it is a P-256 key even for the ES384 and ES512 cases, while the conversion is told to use 48- or 66-byte R/S components and merely zero-pads the P-256 values. It also only asserts concat -> DER -> concat round-tripping with the same implementation under test and never compares the DER result with the original Signature.sign() output or verifies it with Signature.verify(). A standards-incorrect but self-consistent encoder/decoder pair, or incorrect curve-length handling for real P-384/P-521 signatures, can therefore pass; each algorithm should use a key on its corresponding curve and validate against the JCA signature.
